clues.title: Plate: long yellow with blue strip on left
text: Luxembourg uses **long** **yellow** plates with a blue strip on the left.
Since Luxembourg is a small country, foreign cars with [white plates](https://goo.gl/maps/5frYTtwZD81cVohD9) are somewhat common.
NOTE: There are only a few other European countries that use yellow plates for private vehicles:
- The Netherlands has yellow plates front and rear.
- The UK has yellow rear plates.
- Some pre-2009 French cars have yellow rear plates.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Long yellow plates with a blue strip on the left. Foreign cars with white plates are fairly common because the country is small.

differs.how: Dutch plates are yellow front and rear, no blue strip
British plates are yellow only at the rear

clues.title: Bollard: black and white wedge
text: **Bollards** are black and white. They are wedge-shaped and have grey reflectors. Some have a distinctive [indent](https://goo.gl/maps/P4GMqrARAYXyAqRYA) in the lower half.

NOTE: They look more or less identical to [German](https://goo.gl/maps/6ELNoXaCi3LPUiML9) bollards. The most notable difference is that the reflectors on German bollards have two bolts, while in Luxembourg they have [three](https://goo.gl/maps/w92yU6hXM4GRDrH58).
The bollards of Belgium, the Netherlands and France look very different.

images.caption: Wedge bollard: left shot is the back with two round reflectors, F = front with arrows and 3 marking its reflector
German-style wedge bollard: F = front with a rectangular reflector (arrows marked 2), B = back

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black and white wedge-shaped bollard with a grey reflector, sometimes with an indent in the lower half. Looks like the German one, but the reflector has three bolts instead of two.

differs.how: German reflector has two bolts, not three

clues.title: Chevron: black with yellow arrows
text: Chevrons are **black with yellow** arrows. You may also rarely come across [blue and yellow](https://www.google.com/maps/@49.6287886,6.1349694,3a,15y,1.97h,71.47t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1s64mNrisMtRf0qKgQ49PAaw!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu) chevrons.
NOTE: None of Luxembourg’s neighbours use these chevrons.
The only other European countries with this colour scheme tend to have wildly different landscapes: Iceland, Norway, Finland, Ireland, and Portugal.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Black chevron boards with yellow arrows, rarely blue and yellow. No neighbour uses these, so it points to Luxembourg unless the landscape says Iceland, Norway, Finland, Ireland or Portugal.

differs.how: Same colours but a very different landscape
Same colours but a very different landscape

clues.title: Pole: upside-down trident top
text: Poles with poletops shaped like **upside-down tridents** are the most common type of pole in Luxembourg.
In addition, you can find a variety of other poletops.
NOTE: These poles can also be commonly seen in France, Spain and Portugal.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The most common pole has a top shaped like an upside-down trident, with other tops mixed in. France, Spain and Portugal have it too.

clues.title: Coverage: Gen 2 or Gen 4 camera
text: Almost all coverage in Luxembourg is either **Generation 2 or Generation 4**.
Generation 3 is rare, but [does exist](https://goo.gl/maps/DVuUian1XUX3BSL1A).

images.caption: The same city avenue in Gen 2 camera quality (left) and Gen 4 (right)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Nearly all coverage is from the Gen 2 or Gen 4 camera. The older, blurrier Gen 3 exists but is rare.

clues.title: Language: French most, then German
text: Luxembourg is a highly **multilingual country**. It has three administrative languages: Luxembourgish, French, and German.
French is the language that is mostly used for public communication. Road signs and advertisements are usually in French.
Presence of German on signs is less common compared to French, but certainly not non-existent.

images.caption: French direction sign on the left beside a German-language warning sign on the right

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Three official languages, but French is used most on road signs and adverts. German on signs is less common, though not rare.

clues.title: Language: German-looking with doubled vowels
text: **Luxembourgish** is closely related to German and can look very similar. Like German, it uses umlauts (dots over vowels). In addition, it uses a fair amount of double vowels, and sometimes an é with an accent.
Most town names have their origin in Luxembourgish, German, or both.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Looks like German, with umlauts, lots of double vowels and sometimes an accented é. Most town names come from Luxembourgish, German, or both.

clues.title: Sign: yellow framed direction signs
text: **Directional signs **are yellow with a thin black outline. Town names are written in uppercase. The signs have a pointed tip. They are completely surrounded by a **frame**, making them very recognizable.
Some directional signs feature road numbers:
- Regional road numbers have 1 or 2 digits and a red box.
- Local road numbers have 3 digits and a [yellow box](https://goo.gl/maps/vunmzYKY3iy5bEGk6).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Yellow direction signs with a thin black outline, a pointed tip and a full frame around them. Town names are in capitals. Road numbers sit in a red box (1-2 digits) or a yellow box (3 digits).

clues.title: Sign: yellow framed town entrance
text: **Town entrance signs **are also yellow and surrounded by a frame.
Most of these signs have bilingual versions of the town name. They frequently have the road number on the top, along with a speed limit sign.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Town entrance signs are yellow with a frame around them, usually with the town name in two languages. The road number and a speed limit often sit on top.

clues.title: Road signs: square-cornered frames
text: The **frames **mentioned in the previous two tips are also commonly found on a lot of other road infrastructure.

NOTE: Denmark notably also uses a lot of similar-looking frames on road infrastructure. A recognizable difference is that the corners on Luxembourg frames are more square, while Danish frames are more [rounded](https://goo.gl/maps/58VmxHoeLNTXUUNM8).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Frames like those on the direction signs appear on lots of other road items. Denmark has similar frames, but its corners are rounder, while these are more square.

differs.how: Danish frame corners are more rounded

clues.title: Sign: white signposts
text: Almost all Luxembourgish road signs will be supported by a **white signpost**.
NOTE: While not nearly as common, white signposts are also found in [France](https://maps.app.goo.gl/rYufTJHHu99ALVKf6).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Almost all road signs are mounted on white signposts. France has some too, but much less often.

clues.title: Street sign: short, white, slanted blue corners
text: **Street signs** are almost always short and usually have a white background. The exact designs vary from town to town.
A very common design is the one pictured on the left in the example image, with slanted blue corners.
NOTE: Belgian street signs often appear short as well, but can have other background colours – not just white.
In addition, Dutch street signs almost always have a blue background and tend to be much longer than they are tall.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Street name signs are short and mostly white, with designs varying by town. A common one has slanted blue corners.

differs.how: Belgian ones are also short but can be other colours
Dutch ones are blue, long and low

clues.title: Signpost: bulky blue-and-white round reflector
text: Some signposts have this bulky, round reflector with **blue and white** markings.
NOTE: Similar markings are found in Sweden and Finland. Landscape should be sufficient to tell these apart from Luxembourg, however.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some signposts carry a bulky round reflector with blue and white markings. Sweden and Finland have similar ones, but the landscape tells them apart.

clues.title: Sign: pedestrian crossing, 5 vertical stripes
text: **Pedestrian signs** have 5 vertical stripes.
NOTE: Belgian pedestrian signs have 2 horizontal stripes.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The pedestrian crossing sign shows 5 vertical stripes. Belgian ones have 2 horizontal stripes.

clues.title: Sign: blue bus stop, bus with six windows
text: **Bus stop signs** are blue and always have this exact design. The bus has six windows.
NOTE: Bus stop signs in Belgium and the Netherlands have significantly different designs. For example, the Belgian bus stop sign always has a [yellow signpost](https://goo.gl/maps/HRqx4mPFRvtkV2u2A).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Bus stop signs are blue and always the same design, with a bus that has six windows. Belgian and Dutch ones look quite different; the Belgian one has a yellow post.

differs.how: Belgian bus stop sign has a different design and yellow post
Dutch bus stop sign has a different design

clues.title: Landscape: green rolling hills
text: Almost all of Luxembourg’s landscape consists of green **rolling hills**, with a patchwork of agriculture and forests.
NOTE: If you see a yellow licence plate, and you are not sure what country it belongs to, landscape is often a good clue: almost all of the Netherlands is completely flat.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Nearly everywhere is green rolling hills with a patchwork of farmland and forest. If you see yellow plates and are unsure, hills rule out the Netherlands, which is flat.

clues.title: Houses: dark slate roofs, plain walls
text: Houses tend to have **dark slate roofs**.
Walls and windows tend to be plain and undecorated. Walls are usually painted white, grey, or pastel colours.
NOTE: Such architecture can also be found in the surrounding regions in Belgium and France, but is especially prominent in Luxembourg.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Houses have dark slate roofs and plain walls painted white, grey or pastel. Neighbouring parts of Belgium and France look the same, though it is most common here.

clues.title: Road numbers: 3 digits, first digit by area
text: **Local road numbers** have three digits. They are geographically clustered by first digit. The first digits range from 1-3.
- 1xx is found in the southern half.
- 2xx is found in and around the capital.
- 3xx is found in the northern half.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Local road numbers have three digits starting with 1 in the south, 2 around the capital and 3 in the north.

clues.title: Landscape: hillier, higher north
text: The north of the country is **hillier **and has an overall higher elevation than the south.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The north is hillier and higher than the south.

clues.title: Landscape: vineyards in the southeast
text: **Vineyards** are primarily found in the southeast of the country.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Vineyards are mostly in the southeast of the country.

clues.title: Google car: Gen 3 backpack in city centre
text: Some of Luxembourg City’s downtown area was covered by a **Generation 3 urban trekker**. Occasionally, the trekker’s sunglasses and greying hair can be seen.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Parts of the capital's downtown were shot with a Gen 3 backpack camera. Sometimes you can see the carrier's sunglasses and greying hair.
